subject: 32 banned Nvidia chips showed up on a public dashboard
bodyMarkdown:
Nvidia closed Thursday down 4.4 per cent at $212.21, and the same day a security firm said it had spotted 32 banned Nvidia chips answering to a Chinese state carrier's network. If you own Nvidia inside an index fund, it is worth sorting out which of those two things should change your mind.

## What Lava says it found

The Information reported on Thursday that Lava, an Israeli security firm, identified 32 Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 processors inside the network of China Telecom, the state-owned carrier. Tom's Hardware picked it up Friday. The B300 is one of Nvidia's strongest data centre chips and cannot legally be sold to a Chinese buyer under current US export controls. Lava did not get there through a customs record or a whistleblower. It found Nvidia monitoring instances sitting on the public internet with no authentication, and read the GPU inventory off the dashboard. One caveat: the data does not show where the chips sit, or that China Telecom bought or houses them. Nvidia did not deny the finding. It said **diversion**, the industry word for a chip sold legally in one country and resold into a banned one, runs below 0.5 per cent of deployed inventory, and called it a drop in the bucket next to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.

## Nobody needed a border inspection

Thirty-two chips is a rounding error. Nvidia shipped 678,000 units into China in the first half of this year legally. The method is what I keep turning over. Lava ran four internet scans between March and May and found roughly 2,100 hosts serving GPU monitoring metrics with no password, reporting more than 12,000 unique processors across close to 300 organizations, worth about $100 million by its estimate. The exposed fleet ran from H100s and H200s to consumer RTX 4090 and 5090 cards, including customer deployments at Voltage Park, Lambda, Northern Data and DigitalOcean. The flaw Lava disclosed in the same tooling, CVE-2026-47483, carries an Nvidia severity score of 8.2 and is fixed in DCGM Exporter 4.8.2. So a fleet nobody was supposed to be able to see turned out to be enumerable from a laptop. You do not need a port inspector if the hardware volunteers its own inventory to anyone who asks.

## The bigger China number landed ten days ago

Here is what the smuggling headlines crowd out. Reuters reported on October 13, using IDC data, that Nvidia's share of China's data centre AI accelerator market fell to 34 per cent in the first half of 2026, with Huawei at 28 per cent. Nvidia's shipments into the country dropped 44 per cent from a year earlier. Huawei shipped 572,000 units, up from roughly 300,000. IDC would not say whether its Nvidia figure includes restricted B200 and B300 parts that have reportedly been smuggled in. Put the two stories side by side and the picture inverts. The controls are doing on volume exactly what they were written to do, and Huawei is collecting the difference. Nvidia's China problem is measured in legal sales it no longer makes. Thirty-two leaked chips do not move that line. Thursday's drop came with the whole AI complex, after Meta's results reopened the argument about spending, and had nothing to do with China.

## The takeaway

I would not trade on a smuggling headline, and Thursday's 4.4 per cent slide is the better guide to what moves this stock right now. The figure I am watching is Nvidia's China data centre revenue when it next reports, because that is where a 44 per cent shipment drop finally shows up in dollars instead of units. If you run GPUs anywhere, the free job this weekend is checking whether your monitoring endpoints answer strangers, then upgrading DCGM Exporter to 4.8.2. Longer term, watch whether Washington shifts from policing physical boxes to policing remote access, the gap this episode points at.
